headline: Chancellor Healey faces halved buffer ahead of 28 October Budget

terms.meaning: The gap between what the government plans to borrow and the limit it has set itself.
Bonds the UK government sells to borrow money.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the public finances.

levels.headline: Chancellor Healey faces halved buffer ahead of 28 October Budget
levels.body:
The Autumn Budget will be delivered on Wednesday 28 October 2026 by Chancellor John Healey, who took the job a little over three months ago under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the independent forecaster, will publish its updated economic and fiscal forecast on the same day. Mr Healey confirmed the date in a letter to the Treasury Select Committee published on 31 July.
PwC estimates that movements in government bond yields and interest rates have roughly halved the Chancellor's fiscal headroom, the buffer between his plans and his own borrowing rules, to about £14 billion. Higher yields mean the government pays more to borrow, which eats into that buffer.
The government has repeated its manifesto promise not to raise income tax rates, and income tax thresholds are already frozen until April 2031. Commentators therefore expect attention to fall on other taxes, such as capital gains tax, while large-company corporation tax is expected to stay at 25%. Coverage also expects a roadmap giving mayors a bigger share of locally raised revenue, starting with business rates.
levels.why: It shows how higher borrowing costs limit what the government can spend or cut, and so what taxes may do.

levels.headline: Chancellor Healey's fiscal buffer halves before the Autumn Budget
levels.body:
The Autumn Budget is due on Wednesday 28 October, and the Chancellor, John Healey, has less room to manoeuvre than expected. He took the job a little over three months ago under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The OBR, the official forecaster, will publish new forecasts on the same day.
PwC estimates that changes in bond yields and interest rates have roughly halved his fiscal headroom, the cushion between his plans and his borrowing rules, to about £14 billion. When yields rise, the cost of government borrowing goes up with them.
Ministers have repeated their pledge not to raise income tax rates, and thresholds stay frozen until April 2031. Analysts therefore point to capital gains tax as a possible target, while corporation tax for large firms is expected to stay at 25%. A plan for mayors to keep more local revenue, beginning with business rates, is also expected.
levels.why: It shows how rising borrowing costs squeeze the choices open to the Chancellor.

levels.headline: Budget buffer shrinks as borrowing costs rise
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. He has been in the job for a little over three months, serving under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility will publish fresh forecasts at the same time.
According to PwC, rising bond yields and interest rates have roughly halved the government's headroom, the margin by which it meets its own borrowing rules, to around £14 billion. Put simply, borrowing has become more expensive, so there is less spare money.
The government says it will not raise income tax rates, and the thresholds at which people start paying tax are frozen until April 2031. That leaves other taxes in the spotlight, including capital gains tax. Large companies are expected to keep paying corporation tax at 25%. A plan to let mayors keep more of the money raised in their areas is also expected.
levels.why: Higher borrowing costs can shape taxes and spending that affect households.

levels.headline: Chancellor has less room for manoeuvre before Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will present the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October, just over three months after taking the job under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility, will publish new predictions the same day.
PwC estimates that the government's financial cushion, known as headroom, has roughly halved to about £14 billion. The reason is that the interest the government pays on its borrowing has risen as bond yields have gone up.
Ministers have repeated their promise not to raise income tax rates, and the thresholds for paying it stay frozen until April 2031. Analysts expect attention to turn to other taxes, such as capital gains tax, while corporation tax for large firms should stay at 25%. Mayors may also be offered a bigger share of the tax raised locally.
levels.why: It affects what the Budget can offer and who may pay more tax.

levels.headline: The Chancellor has less spare money before the Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will give the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. He has held the job for a little over three months, working for Prime Minister Andy Burnham. On the same day, an independent group called the Office for Budget Responsibility will share its forecasts for the economy.
The firm PwC says the government's spare room for borrowing, called headroom, has roughly halved to about £14 billion. This is because the interest the government pays on its loans has gone up. Think of it as a household whose monthly bills have grown, leaving less to spend freely.
The government says it will not put up income tax rates, and the levels at which people start paying tax are frozen until April 2031. So experts think other taxes, like capital gains tax, could be looked at. Big companies should keep paying 25% corporation tax, which is tax on their profits.
levels.why: It could affect your taxes, public services and prices.

levels.headline: The Budget is coming and the government has less spare cash
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will give the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. This is the government's yearly plan for taxes and spending. He has held the job for a little over three months. An independent group called the OBR will share its forecasts for the economy on the same day.
The company PwC says the government now has less spare room for borrowing. This is called headroom. It has roughly halved to about £14 billion. The reason is that the interest the government pays on what it borrows has gone up, so more of its money goes on bills.
The government says it will not raise income tax rates, and the point at which people start paying tax is frozen until April 2031. So experts think other taxes, such as capital gains tax, could change. Capital gains tax is paid on the profit from selling things like shares. Large companies should keep paying 25% on their profits.
levels.why: It affects taxes, public services and what the government can afford.

levels.headline: The Budget is on 28 October and there is less spare money
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will give the Autumn Budget on Wednesday 28 October. A Budget is when the government says how it will raise money through tax and how it will spend it. He started the job a little over three months ago. An independent team, the OBR, will share new forecasts that day.
The firm PwC says the government's safety cushion has shrunk. This cushion, called headroom, is the gap between what the government plans to borrow and the limit it has set itself. It has roughly halved to about £14 billion. The reason is that borrowing now costs more in interest.
The government says it will not raise income tax rates. The point at which people start paying tax is also frozen until April 2031. Experts think other taxes, such as capital gains tax, may go up instead. That is tax on the profit when you sell something like shares. Large companies should keep paying 25% tax on their profits.
levels.why: It matters because Budgets decide how much tax people pay.

levels.headline: The Chancellor has less money to play with before the Budget
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, the Chancellor will give the Budget. The Chancellor is the minister in charge of the country's money. His name is John Healey. A Budget is a big speech about taxes and spending. A group of experts called the OBR will also give its forecasts.
A company called PwC says the government now has less spare money. Experts call this spare money headroom. It is about £14 billion, which is about half what it was. The government borrows money by selling bonds, and it must pay interest on them. Lately that interest has gone up.
The government says it will not raise income tax. This is the tax taken from people's pay. The level at which people start paying it is frozen until April 2031. Experts think other taxes may rise, like tax on the profit made from selling shares. Big firms should keep paying 25% on their profits.
levels.why: It matters because the Budget decides how money is shared out.

levels.headline: Why the Budget is a worry this month
levels.body:
The Chancellor will give a big speech on 28 October. It is called the Budget. The Chancellor is the person in charge of the country's money. His name is John Healey. In the speech he says what taxes will be and how money will be spent. Taxes are money people pay to the government.
The government has less spare money than before. Spare money means the money left over after it has made its plans. A company called PwC says it is now about £14 billion. That is about half as much as before. The government borrows money, and it pays extra, called interest. That extra has got bigger.
The government says it will not make income tax bigger. Income tax is the money taken from people's pay. People start paying it above a set amount, and that amount will stay the same until 2031. Experts think some other taxes could go up. Big companies will keep paying the same tax.
levels.why: It matters because the Budget affects how much families pay and get.

levels.headline: A grown-up has less spare pocket money
levels.body:
Imagine a country has a big money jar. Once in a while, the leader of the money, called the Chancellor, tells everyone how the jar will be filled and spent. His name is John Healey. That big talk is called the Budget, and it happens on 28 October.
This time the jar has less spare money in it. Think of pocket money. If you borrowed some from a friend, you would have to pay back a little extra. The government borrowed money too, and the little extra has grown. So there is less left over to spend on nice things.
The government has said it will not take more money from people's wages. Some other taxes might change, though. Grown-ups will be listening closely to the speech. It matters because taxes pay for things like schools, hospitals and roads.
levels.why: It shows that even a government has to be careful with money.

headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as three members vote to raise it

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences what banks charge and pay.
The nine-member group that votes on interest rates.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as three members vote to raise it
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 on 17 September 2026 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%. Three members, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, wanted a quarter-point rise to 4%. The other six, including Governor Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Swati Dhingra, Clare Lombardelli, Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor, voted to hold.
Bank Rate has not moved since a quarter-point cut from 4% on 18 December 2025. The Bank said energy prices remain volatile because of the conflict in the Middle East, and that this means inflation, currently 3.1%, will rise further.
The next decision is due on Thursday 5 November 2026, alongside a new Monetary Policy Report. Commentators say a rise is becoming increasingly likely if energy prices stay high. Bank Rate influences the cost of mortgages and loans and the return on savings, so any move matters to millions of households.
levels.why: It sets the price of borrowing for mortgages and loans, and three votes for a rise hint that rates could go up on 5 November.

levels.headline: Bank of England keeps rates at 3.75% despite three votes for a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England voted 6-3 on 17 September to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%. Three members of the Monetary Policy Committee, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, wanted a quarter-point rise to 4%. Governor Andrew Bailey and five colleagues voted to hold.
Bank Rate has stayed put since a quarter-point cut in December 2025. The Bank said energy prices are still volatile because of the Middle East conflict, and that inflation, now 3.1%, is likely to rise further.
The next decision is on Thursday 5 November, when the Bank will also publish a new Monetary Policy Report. Some commentators say a rise is increasingly likely if energy prices stay high. Bank Rate feeds through to mortgage rates, loan costs and the interest paid on savings.
levels.why: It signals that rates may rise if energy-driven inflation persists, with the next decision on 5 November.

levels.headline: Bank of England holds interest rates, but three want a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England has left its main interest rate, Bank Rate, at 3.75% after a 6-3 vote on 17 September. Three members of its rate-setting committee, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, argued for a rise to 4%, while six others, including Governor Andrew Bailey, wanted to wait.
The rate has not changed since a cut in December 2025. The Bank said energy prices remain unpredictable because of the fighting in the Middle East. It expects inflation, currently 3.1%, to climb further because of this.
The next decision comes on 5 November, along with a new report on the Bank's forecasts. Some commentators think a rise is increasingly likely if energy stays expensive. Changes to Bank Rate affect mortgage costs, loan costs and what savers earn.
levels.why: It affects mortgages, loans and savings, and a rise may be coming.

levels.headline: Bank of England keeps rates unchanged as energy prices bite
levels.body:
The Bank of England has decided to keep its main interest rate at 3.75%. The vote on 17 September was 6-3. Three members of the committee that sets rates, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, wanted a small rise to 4%. The other six, led by Governor Andrew Bailey, preferred to wait.
The rate has stayed the same since a small cut in December 2025. The Bank said energy prices are still jumping around because of the conflict in the Middle East, so it expects inflation, the speed at which prices rise, to go higher than the current 3.1%.
The next decision is on 5 November. Some analysts say a rise looks more likely if energy prices stay high. The rate matters because it helps decide what people pay on mortgages and loans and what they earn on savings.
levels.why: It affects what people pay on mortgages and earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England left interest rates where they are
levels.body:
The Bank of England has kept its main interest rate at 3.75%. This is the rate that guides how much banks charge for loans and pay on savings. The decision was made on 17 September and was not unanimous. Three of the nine people who vote, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, wanted to raise it to 4%. The other six wanted to wait.
The rate has not changed since a small cut last December. The Bank is worried because energy prices keep jumping around, partly because of the war in the Middle East. Higher energy costs push up prices in shops, so inflation, now 3.1%, is expected to rise.
The Bank will decide again on 5 November. Some experts think a rise is quite likely if energy stays expensive. A higher rate would make mortgages and loans cost more, but savers could earn more too.
levels.why: It affects mortgage payments and savings returns.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has not changed its main interest rate
levels.body:
The Bank of England has decided not to change its main interest rate, which stays at 3.75%. This rate guides what banks charge on mortgages and loans and what they pay on savings. On 17 September, six of the nine people who vote chose to keep it. Three, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, wanted a small rise to 4%.
Prices are rising partly because energy costs keep jumping, linked to the war in the Middle East. The Bank thinks inflation, now 3.1%, will go higher.
It will decide again on 5 November. Some experts think a rise may come then. That would make loans and mortgages cost more, and it could help people who save.
levels.why: It affects loans, mortgages and savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England kept interest rates the same
levels.body:
The Bank of England has decided to keep interest rates the same at 3.75%. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. The Bank sets a main rate that other banks follow. Nine people vote on it. On 17 September, six voted to keep it. Three wanted to put it up a little, to 4%.
The rate has been the same since last December. The Bank is worried about energy, like petrol and gas. Prices for these keep changing, partly because of a war in the Middle East. When energy costs more, shop prices rise too. This is called inflation. It is now 3.1%, and the Bank thinks it will go higher.
The Bank will vote again on 5 November. Some experts think the rate might go up then. If it does, loans and mortgages would cost more. People with savings might earn a bit more.
levels.why: It matters because interest rates change what loans cost.

levels.headline: The Bank of England decided not to change interest rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England has chosen not to change interest rates. The rate stays at 3.75%. Interest is extra money you pay when you borrow money. The Bank of England sets a main rate for the whole country. Nine people at the Bank vote on it. Six voted to keep it the same. Three wanted it to go up a little.
The rate has stayed the same since last December. The Bank is worried about the cost of energy, like petrol. It changes a lot because of a war far away. When petrol costs more, other things cost more too. This is called inflation. The Bank thinks prices will rise faster soon.
The Bank will vote again on 5 November. Some experts think the rate may go up. If it does, borrowing money will cost more. Families with a mortgage might pay more each month. People who save money might get a little more.
levels.why: It matters because interest rates change what borrowing costs.

levels.headline: The Bank of England said no to changing interest rates
levels.body:
The Bank of England is in charge of a big number called the interest rate. It is 3.75%. The Bank looks after the money of the whole country. Interest is extra money you pay if you borrow. If you save, you get a little extra. The Bank chose to keep the number the same. Six people voted to keep it. Three wanted it higher.
Why did they wait? Prices are going up. Petrol and gas cost more because of a war far away. When they cost more, many things in shops cost more too. The Bank wants prices to stay steady, so it watches them very closely.
The Bank will choose again on 5 November. It might raise the number then. If it did, borrowing would cost more. Many families borrow money to buy their homes. So a small change can matter to a lot of people.
levels.why: It matters because it changes how much families pay on loans.

levels.headline: The people in charge of money rates chose to wait
levels.body:
Imagine a big bank that is in charge of how much extra you pay when you borrow. That extra is called interest. It is like a small fee. The Bank of England said it will keep the fee the same for now. Six wise people said keep it. Three said make it a bit bigger.
Why are they being careful? Petrol and heating cost more because of a war far away. When those cost more, sweets and toys can cost more too. Grown-ups call this prices going up. The Bank wants prices to calm down.
They will talk again on 5 November. They might make the fee bigger. If they do, borrowing costs more for families. It is a bit like if the school tuck shop raised its prices. Everyone would have to think about what to buy.
levels.why: It matters because it changes how much loans cost.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% in August as fuel prices climb

terms.meaning: The Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of inflation.
Inflation leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
A version of CPI that also counts the cost of owning and running a home.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% in August as fuel prices climb
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said. CPIH, which includes the costs of owning a home, rose to 3.3% from 3.1%. The biggest upward pressure came from petrol and diesel, with diesel prices up 14.2 pence per litre in August to an average of 181.8 pence.
Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.6%, unchanged from July. Services inflation held at 3.4%. Goods prices rose 2.7%, the fastest since September 2025, while food inflation stayed at 1.3%.
Inflation fell in the first half of 2026 to a low of 2.6% in June but has risen in recent months. The Bank of England has said it expects inflation to rise further because of volatile energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict. The ONS publishes September's figures on 21 October.
levels.why: It shows how the energy shock is feeding into prices, and may push the Bank of England towards raising rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as petrol and diesel push prices up
levels.body:
Inflation, the rate at which prices rise, climbed to 3.1% in the year to August 2026, from 2.9% in July, according to the ONS. A wider measure that includes housing costs, CPIH, rose to 3.3%. Petrol and diesel were the biggest drivers: diesel rose 14.2 pence per litre in August to an average of 181.8 pence.
Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was steady at 2.6%, and services inflation also held at 3.4%. Prices of goods rose 2.7%, the fastest since September 2025. Food inflation stayed at 1.3%.
The rate dropped to 2.6% in June but has crept up since. The Bank of England expects it to rise further as energy prices remain volatile because of the Middle East conflict. The next figures, for September, are due on 21 October.
levels.why: It shows fuel costs lifting overall inflation and may influence the next interest rate decision.

levels.headline: Inflation edges up to 3.1% as fuel costs rise
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August, up from 2.9% in July, official figures show. CPIH, which also counts the cost of housing, was 3.3%. The main cause was fuel. Diesel went up by 14.2 pence a litre in August, reaching an average of 181.8 pence.
Core inflation, which ignores energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, stayed at 2.6%, and prices for services rose 3.4%, also unchanged. The cost of goods rose 2.7%, the fastest pace since September last year. Food prices rose just 1.3%.
Inflation had dropped to 2.6% in June but has risen since. The Bank of England expects it to go higher still, because energy prices keep jumping around while the Middle East conflict continues. Figures for September come out on 21 October.
levels.why: It affects the cost of living and interest-rate decisions.

levels.headline: UK inflation rose to 3.1% in August, driven by fuel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK rose 3.1% over the year to August, faster than the 2.9% seen in July, the Office for National Statistics reports. Another measure that includes housing costs, called CPIH, was 3.3%. Fuel was the main reason. Diesel went up 14.2 pence a litre in August to an average of 181.8 pence.
Core inflation, which leaves out the most changeable items such as energy and food, stayed at 2.6%. Services such as haircuts and train fares rose 3.4%. Goods rose 2.7%, the fastest in almost a year. Food prices rose only 1.3%.
Inflation was as low as 2.6% in June, but it has been climbing since. The Bank of England thinks it will keep rising because energy prices are uncertain during the Middle East conflict. The next figures are due on 21 October.
levels.why: It affects the cost of living and what interest rates do next.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, with fuel the main cause
levels.body:
UK inflation, the rate at which prices rise, went up to 3.1% in the year to August, from 2.9% in July. The Office for National Statistics says fuel was the main reason: diesel cost 14.2 pence more per litre in August, at an average of 181.8 pence. A wider measure that includes housing costs was 3.3%.
Prices excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco rose 2.6%, the same as in July. Services rose 3.4% and food only 1.3%. Goods rose 2.7%, the fastest since September last year.
Inflation fell to 2.6% in June but has been rising since. The Bank of England expects it to go higher because energy prices are unsteady during the Middle East conflict. The next figures are due on 21 October.
levels.why: It means your money buys a little less, and rates could rise.

levels.headline: Prices rose faster in August because of petrol and diesel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are rising a little faster. The Office for National Statistics says prices were 3.1% higher in August than a year earlier. In July the figure was 2.9%. This rise in prices is called inflation. A second measure, which also counts the cost of housing, was 3.3%. The main cause was fuel. A litre of diesel cost 14.2 pence more in August, at an average of 181.8 pence.
If you leave out things whose prices jump around, like energy and food, inflation was 2.6%, the same as in July. Services, such as haircuts, rose 3.4%. Food prices rose just 1.3%.
In June inflation was only 2.6%, so it has been going up since then. The Bank of England thinks it will rise more, because energy prices are unsteady during the war in the Middle East. New figures come out on 21 October.
levels.why: It means money buys a little less than before.

levels.headline: Prices went up faster in August, mostly because of fuel
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are going up a bit faster. This is called inflation. The official number was 3.1% for the year to August. A month before, it was 2.9%. That means something that cost £100 a year ago now costs about £103. The biggest reason was fuel. Diesel went up by 14.2 pence for each litre in August.
Not everything went up the same. Food prices went up only a little, by 1.3%. Services, like haircuts, went up 3.4%. If you take out fuel, food and some other items, the rise was 2.6%. That was the same as in July.
In June, the number was lower, at 2.6%. It has been rising since. The Bank of England thinks it will go higher. This is because fuel prices keep jumping, partly due to a war in the Middle East. The next number comes out on 21 October.
levels.why: It matters because rising prices make money go less far.

levels.headline: Prices are going up a bit faster, and petrol is the reason
levels.body:
Prices in the shops are going up a bit faster. Grown-ups call this inflation. The number was 3.1% for the year to August. That means something that cost £100 last year now costs about £103. The main reason is petrol and diesel. They cost much more than before. A litre of diesel went up by 14.2 pence in one month.
Not everything went up by the same amount. Food went up only a little. Services, like haircuts, went up a bit more. In June, prices were rising more slowly. Since then they have sped up again.
The Bank of England thinks prices may rise even more. Fuel costs keep changing because of a war in the Middle East. When fuel costs more, it costs more to move things to shops. So shop prices go up. New numbers will come out on 21 October.
levels.why: It matters because things cost more.

levels.headline: Prices went up faster because fuel costs more
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are going up faster. The number is called inflation, and it is now 3.1%. A year ago, something that cost £100 would now cost about £103. In July the number was 2.9%. Petrol and diesel were the main reason. A litre of diesel cost 14.2 pence more in August.
Not everything rose by the same amount. Food rose only 1.3%. Services, like haircuts, rose 3.4%. In June the rise was smaller, at 2.6%.
The Bank of England thinks prices will go up faster still, because fuel keeps changing in cost during a war in the Middle East. New numbers come out on 21 October.
levels.why: It matters because families have to pay more for things.

levels.headline: Things in the shops cost a bit more, and petrol cost much more
levels.body:
Prices are going up. Grown-ups call this inflation. This year, things cost a little more than last year. If a toy cost £100 last year, it might cost about £103 now. The number is 3.1%. Last month it was a bit lower. The biggest reason is petrol. Petrol and diesel are what cars and lorries use. They cost much more now.
Why does petrol matter? Lorries use it to bring food and toys to shops. If it costs more, the shops pay more, and so we pay more. Some things, like food, have hardly gone up at all. Others, like petrol, have gone up a lot.
The Bank of England watches prices. It thinks they may rise some more. Grown-ups will get new numbers on 21 October. It matters because your pocket money buys a little less when prices go up.
levels.why: It matters because pocket money buys a little less.

headline: UK unemployment at 4.9% with youth rate at 16.4% as new figures loom

terms.meaning: The share of people looking for work who cannot find a job.
Job openings that employers are trying to fill.
The share of people aged 16 to 64 who are neither working nor looking for work.

levels.headline: UK unemployment at 4.9% with youth rate at 16.4% as new figures loom
levels.body:
UK unemployment stood at 4.9% in the three months to July 2026, with 1.78 million people out of work, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). That is 83,000 more than a year earlier, when the rate was 4.7%. Among 16-to-24-year-olds the rate was 16.4%, up from 14.3% a year before.
The inactivity rate for people aged 16 to 64, meaning those neither working nor looking for work, was 20.9%. Job vacancies fell over the year to 702,000 in June to August 2026, below their level before the pandemic.
The ONS will publish the next labour market figures, covering June to August 2026, at 7am on Tuesday 20 October. The numbers matter to the Bank of England, which is weighing inflation against the health of the jobs market, and to the Chancellor ahead of the Autumn Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: Weak hiring hits young people hardest, and new figures on 20 October will show whether the trend is worsening.

levels.headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% while youth joblessness reaches 16.4%
levels.body:
Unemployment was 4.9% in the three months to July, according to the ONS, equal to 1.78 million people and 83,000 more than a year earlier, when the rate was 4.7%. For 16-to-24-year-olds the rate was 16.4%, compared with 14.3% a year before.
Some 20.9% of people aged 16 to 64 were economically inactive, neither working nor seeking work. Vacancies dropped over the year to 702,000 in June to August, which is below the level seen before the pandemic.
The next release, covering June to August, is due at 7am on 20 October. It will be watched by the Bank of England, which must balance rising inflation against a softening jobs market, and by the Chancellor ahead of the Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: The figures show a weakening labour market ahead of new data on 20 October.

levels.headline: Jobless rate 4.9% as young people struggle to find work
levels.body:
The unemployment rate was 4.9% in the three months to July, the ONS says. That is 1.78 million people, 83,000 more than a year earlier, when the rate was 4.7%. Young people were hit hardest: 16.4% of 16-to-24-year-olds were unemployed, up from 14.3%.
Around one in five people aged 16 to 64 were not working and not looking for work, an inactivity rate of 20.9%. Job vacancies fell to 702,000 in June to August, which is lower than before the pandemic.
The next figures, covering June to August, are published at 7am on 20 October. The Bank of England will study them as it weighs rising prices against a weakening jobs market, and the Chancellor will do the same ahead of the Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: It shows how hard it is becoming to find work, especially for the young.

levels.headline: Unemployment at 4.9% as youth jobless rate climbs
levels.body:
Unemployment in the UK was 4.9% in the three months to July, the Office for National Statistics reports. That means 1.78 million people were out of work, which is 83,000 more than a year before. The biggest problem is among the young. For people aged 16 to 24, 16.4% were unemployed, up from 14.3%.
About 20.9% of people aged 16 to 64 were not in work and not looking for it. Employers had fewer jobs on offer too. Vacancies fell to 702,000 in June to August, below the level before the pandemic.
New figures for June to August arrive at 7am on 20 October. The Bank of England will watch them closely, because it has to weigh rising prices against a weaker jobs market. The Chancellor will also take note before the Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: It shows how hard it is to find work, especially for young people.

levels.headline: More people are out of work, especially the young
levels.body:
Official figures show that 4.9% of people who want a job cannot find one. That is the unemployment rate, for the three months to July. It means about 1.78 million people, which is 83,000 more than a year ago. Young people have found it hardest. Among those aged 16 to 24, 16.4% have no job, compared with 14.3% a year ago.
Many other adults are not working and not looking for work, for example because they are studying or are unwell. Employers also have fewer jobs on offer. Vacancies, meaning open jobs, dropped to 702,000.
New figures come out at 7am on 20 October. They matter because the Bank of England uses them when it decides on interest rates. The Chancellor will also look at them before the Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: It matters for young people looking for their first jobs.

Employers are also offering fewer jobs. Vacancies, meaning job openings, fell to 702,000, below the level before the pandemic. Many other adults are neither working nor looking for work.
New figures come out on 20 October. The Bank of England will use them when it decides on interest rates, and the Chancellor will look at them before the Budget on 28 October.
levels.why: It matters because jobs affect how families get by.

levels.why: It matters because people need work to earn money.

levels.headline: More people are out of work, and many are young

levels.why: It matters because jobs help families buy what they need.

levels.headline: More grown-ups and teenagers cannot find jobs
levels.body:

Young people, like teenagers and those just out of school or college, find it hardest. There are fewer chairs for them. Companies are not hiring as many new people.
New numbers come out on 20 October. Important people will study them. Jobs matter because a job gives people money for food, homes and fun things. The people in charge want everyone who wants a job to find one.
levels.why: It matters because grown-ups need jobs to look after their families.

headline: Burnham tells MPs of Germany partnership on hybrid threats

terms.meaning: Attacks that mix tools such as cyber attacks, spying and false information instead of open warfare.
Protecting people from deliberate false information.
Prime Minister's Questions, the weekly session where MPs question the PM.

levels.headline: Burnham tells MPs of Germany partnership on hybrid threats
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham made an oral statement to the House of Commons on 12 October 2026 reporting on his trip to the UN General Assembly and related international events. He told MPs about a new partnership with Germany to counter hybrid threats, and about plans for a National Centre for Information Defence.
Hybrid threats are hostile actions that fall short of open war, such as cyber attacks, covert interference and deliberate disinformation. The details in the published statement concern the partnership with Germany and the planned centre, which is intended to strengthen the UK's defences against false information.
Mr Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026. MPs can question him at Prime Minister's Questions, which the Commons timetable lists for midday on Wednesday 14 October, with the next session on 21 October.
levels.why: It shows how the new government is approaching security, and MPs can question the PM at PMQs on 14 October.

headline: Burnham government trails cost-of-living measures before the Budget

terms.meaning: Value Added Tax, a tax added to the price of most goods and services.
A tax paid by firms on non-home buildings such as shops and pubs.
Passing powers from central government to local areas.

levels.headline: Burnham government trails cost-of-living measures before the Budget
levels.body:
Ahead of the Autumn Budget on 28 October, several measures have been announced by Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. Coverage lists a £2 cap on bus fares, the removal of VAT from household electricity bills, and a business rates tax cut for pubs and clubs. A House of Lords Library briefing says the VAT change was planned for October 2026.
Reports say the electricity VAT cut would be funded by scrapping the previous government's planned digital ID scheme. At Labour's conference, Mr Burnham also announced plans to remove the Thatcher-era ban on government ownership of water companies and to give councils more power over rogue landlords and empty homes.
The announcements reflect a focus on devolving power to local areas and easing living costs. Budget previews also expect a roadmap letting mayors keep a bigger share of locally raised revenue, starting with business rates. Details of how measures are funded are due at the Budget.
levels.why: It shows how Prime Minister Burnham is trying to ease household bills before the Budget on 28 October.

headline: Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end the war on Iran stall

terms.meaning: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman through which much of the world's oil is shipped.
Stopping ships from entering or leaving a place.
US elections held halfway through a president's term, on 3 November this year.

levels.headline: Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end the war on Iran stall
levels.body:
Attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz have intensified while mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked, Al Jazeera reported on 11 October. Iran wants a June memorandum of understanding, which has since collapsed, to be restored, along with US backing for an Iran-Oman arrangement on entry and exit routes through the strait. Al Jazeera said no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks, before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Shipping has been badly hit. Kpler data cited by CNBC put crude oil transit through the strait for the week ended 7 October about 40 per cent below normal. A tanker was struck in the strait, and Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia killed people, including an American, according to Jerusalem Post live coverage.
A war tracker reports that President Donald Trump said on 8 October the US would not attack Iran before the midterms while keeping its blockade in place.
levels.why: Disruption to the strait keeps oil prices high, which affects petrol, inflation and interest rates around the world.

headline: US 10-year Treasury yield hits highest since 2002 before easing

terms.meaning: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow, which moves opposite to bond prices.
The US central bank.
The Fed committee that sets US interest rates.

levels.headline: US 10-year Treasury yield hits highest since 2002 before easing
levels.body:
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note rose to its highest level since 2002 at the start of the week beginning 5 October, CNBC reported, before a weak September jobs report pulled yields lower. CNBC said the yield briefly touched 5.70%, although FRED data shows a close of about 5.31% that day. By 9 October the 10-year yield was around 5.24%, the 2-year about 4.80% and the 30-year about 5.60%, according to market data trackers.
The Federal Reserve's target range stands at 3.75% to 4.00%. Traders put about an 82% chance on the Fed holding rates at its next meeting, which is on 27 and 28 October, and futures price a rise to about 4.1% by January 2027.
The moves follow a period of higher oil prices tied to the conflict around Iran. US inflation data for September is due on Wednesday 14 October, and big banks including JPMorgan report earnings on Tuesday.
levels.why: US yields set the pace for borrowing costs worldwide, including UK gilts and mortgages.

levels.headline: Brent crude trades near $100 a barrel, up about 57% on a year ago
levels.body:
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, traded around $102.60 a barrel on 5 October 2026, according to Trading Economics, about 57% higher than a year earlier. On 6 October Databoks reported Brent at $100.53 and US benchmark WTI at $89.79 in morning trading.
Analysts link the high prices to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage through which a large share of the world's oil is shipped. Talks to end the war on Iran are stalled, and tankers have been attacked in the strait.
Higher oil prices feed through to fuel costs. UK diesel rose 14.2 pence per litre in August to an average of 181.8 pence, which was the biggest contributor to inflation rising to 3.1%. The Bank of England has cited volatile energy prices as a reason it expects inflation to rise further.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, diesel and inflation, which is why UK prices and interest rates are being affected.

headline: Zelenskyy says Russia broke energy truce as US pushes new peace talks

levels.headline: Zelenskyy says Russia broke energy truce as US pushes new peace talks
levels.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 11 October that Russia had violated an energy truce announced by US President Donald Trump, Al Jazeera reported. The claim followed a diesel deal announced by Mr Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Ukraine bombed a Russian fuel site hours after the announcement, and a Republican senator has questioned whether the diesel agreement may be illegal.
Fighting continued. Al Jazeera reported that at least 33 people were killed when a Russian strike hit two civilian buses in a city in the Donetsk region, while a Russian guided aerial bomb attack in Kharkiv killed one person on 11 October. The outlet also reported that Ukrainian forces have pushed Russian troops back in parts of Donetsk.
Mr Zelenskyy said the US has proposed fresh trilateral talks by the end of October, and that Ukraine has responded positively.
levels.why: It shows how fragile efforts to end the war are, with US-hosted talks possible by the end of October.

levels.headline: Ukraine says Russia did not keep a promise
